paragraphs: Training changes a neural network’s parameters, but some relationships among those parameters can remain constant along gradient flow, the continuous-time description of gradient-based learning. These conserved quantities help describe implicit bias: the ways an optimization process favors particular solutions even when a large model has many possible ways to fit its data.

This paper develops a unified framework for characterizing such conservation laws in modern architectures. Its scope includes feedforward networks using GELU, SiLU, and SwiGLU activations, multihead attention using sinusoidal or rotary positional encodings, and mixtures of experts with different gating designs. This extends the analysis beyond linear and ReLU networks, where conservation laws are already better understood.

The authors also report experiments supporting the invariants predicted by their theory. The contribution is a way to connect concrete architectural choices with quantities preserved during training dynamics. That makes conservation laws available as a tool for studying contemporary models, while keeping the theoretical focus on gradient flow rather than asserting that every discrete training procedure preserves identical quantities.
icml-2026-conservation-laws-for-modern-n.tldr: A unified framework characterizes conserved quantities in gradient flow for modern activations, positional encodings, and mixture-of-experts architectures.

paragraphs: Building a three-dimensional scene from images involves deciding where to look next as well as reconstructing what has already been observed. Creat3r addresses this camera-selection problem. It begins with a small collection of images and their camera poses, then repeatedly chooses an informative next pose, acquires that image, and updates a reconstruction based on 3D Gaussian splatting.

The selection mechanism uses an intermediate point cloud and a three-dimensional confidence field that estimates reconstruction reliability. Gaussian projection converts this information into confidence and exploration maps for candidate camera poses. These maps help weigh reliable regions against uncertain or unseen areas, so camera selection can account for both existing reconstruction quality and opportunities to collect new information under computational constraints.

In experiments using standard 3D Gaussian splatting, Creat3r consistently improves on the compared baselines while requiring fewer views. The reported gains cover both novel-view image quality, measured with SSIM, and reconstructed surface quality, measured with F1. Together, these results indicate that confidence-guided acquisition can make the collected images more useful for both appearance and geometry.
icml-2026-creat3r-confidence-reaggregati.tldr: Creat3r uses projected reconstruction confidence to choose camera views that improve 3D reconstruction with fewer images.

paragraphs: Cross-modal knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from a teacher operating on one kind of data to a student operating on another. A common obstacle is the need for examples matched across modalities, such as different observations with aligned meaning. This paper develops a framework for transferring knowledge when those paired examples are unavailable.

The authors establish a relationship between teacher and student distributions that identifies two quantities governing effective transfer: feature alignment and label alignment. Feature alignment concerns discrepancies in representations, while label alignment concerns discrepancies in prediction distributions. This separates agreement about how information is represented from agreement about what the models predict.

The resulting method aligns distributions instead of requiring correspondence between individual samples. Its theoretical guarantees support this distribution-based approach, and experiments across multimodal benchmarks report significant improvements over prior methods in both paired and unpaired settings. The practical significance is that paired data need not be the organizing requirement for this form of distillation; representation-level and prediction-level agreement provide another basis for transferring knowledge.
icml-2026-cross-modal-knowledge-distilla.tldr: The paper enables cross-modal distillation without paired examples by aligning teacher and student feature and prediction distributions.

paragraphs: A model can be trained to favor fair predictions without necessarily guaranteeing that its outputs satisfy a specified parity rule. This paper introduces a fairness layer: a differentiable optimization problem appended to the network’s output. When integrated into the network, the layer guarantees the chosen notion of output parity, making that requirement part of the prediction mechanism.

Differentiability matters because the optimization layer participates in training through backpropagation. The authors analyze both its differentiability and stability, addressing how an explicit constraint-enforcing component can work within a neural network. The guarantee concerns the selected output-parity definition, so its meaning is tied to the fairness criterion being enforced.

The paper also addresses streaming predictions, where enforcing fairness separately on very small batches can be overly restrictive. An online primal-dual algorithm instead provides provable aggregate fairness guarantees with arbitrarily small batches. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the layer and streaming algorithm, offering complementary approaches for enforcing parity within model outputs and maintaining fairness across a stream of predictions.
icml-2026-differentiable-optimization-la.tldr: A differentiable fairness layer guarantees a chosen output-parity criterion, while an online algorithm provides aggregate fairness for streaming predictions.

paragraphs: Synthetic tables can support data sharing while differential privacy protects information about the source data. However, matching simple statistical relationships does not necessarily preserve patterns involving many columns together. This paper targets those higher-order correlations, which the authors argue receive insufficient attention from methods focused on low-order marginal query errors.

Tab-PE adapts the Private Evolution framework to tabular data. It repeatedly generates variations of a candidate dataset, scores them privately, and retains high-quality samples for further evolution. Its variation operators are heuristics specialized for tables. This removes the reliance on large foundation models used by the original framework and substantially lowers computational costs.

Experiments on real and simulated datasets show particularly strong results when high-order correlations are present. Relative to AIM, identified as the strongest baseline, Tab-PE improves classification accuracy by up to 10% while running 28 times faster. These findings connect the method’s goal to downstream usefulness: preserving more complex relationships can improve predictive tasks, while inexpensive evolutionary operators make private synthesis more practical.
icml-2026-differentially-private-synthet.tldr: Tab-PE evolves synthetic tables using inexpensive operators and private selection, improving results on data with high-order correlations.

paragraphs: Reasoning models can spend computation on additional reflection after it stops being useful. DyCon addresses this overthinking by treating difficulty as something that changes during a solution. A problem’s initial difficulty estimate may become outdated as the model makes progress, which motivates monitoring the reasoning process itself.

The authors empirically find that evolving difficulty is linearly encoded in representations associated with individual reasoning steps. DyCon uses these latent representations to model difficulty as reasoning unfolds and dynamically control reasoning depth. The framework is training-free, avoiding the task-specific training required by some existing approaches while responding to information available during the current solution.

Experiments span four models from 4 billion to 32 billion parameters and twelve benchmarks covering mathematics, general question answering, and coding. The authors report fewer redundant reasoning steps without sacrificing accuracy or generalization in these evaluations. The result supports using internal, step-level signals to allocate reasoning effort according to the model’s changing progress rather than relying only on a fixed assessment made before reasoning begins.
icml-2026-dycon-dynamic-reasoning-contro.tldr: DyCon uses evolving difficulty signals inside reasoning models to reduce redundant steps without reported accuracy or generalization loss.

paragraphs: A convincing-looking generated video may still violate physics. Evaluating this through visual judgments is subjective, while requiring a generated trajectory to match one reference can reject other physically plausible outcomes. Morpheus instead assesses video generation through conservation laws that apply to the particular physical setting.

The framework includes 130 real-world videos depicting physical phenomena and uses them to condition generation. It combines advances in physics-informed neural networks and vision-language foundation models to evaluate interpretable measures of physical plausibility. Its scope is deliberately controlled Newtonian rigid-body settings, where the relevant laws support quantitative checks rather than judgments based mainly on appearance.

The findings show that contemporary generators struggle to encode physical principles even with advanced prompting and video conditioning, despite producing aesthetically pleasing results. This separates visual realism from the specific physical consistency needed for world modeling. Morpheus therefore contributes an evaluation approach that asks whether generated motion respects known constraints in the tested settings, allowing multiple possible trajectories without treating one observed sequence as the sole valid answer.
icml-2026-evaluating-newtonian-mechanics.tldr: Morpheus evaluates generated videos against conservation laws and finds persistent physical inconsistencies in controlled Newtonian settings.

paragraphs: Different neural-network parameters can implement exactly the same function. These equivalences create symmetries in parameter space, complicating comparisons between trained models. This paper studies those symmetries in Transformers while explicitly accounting for positional encodings, which earlier analyses of vanilla multihead attention largely left out.

The authors compare sinusoidal positional encodings with rotary positional encodings, or RoPE. They show that sinusoidal encodings retain vanilla attention’s equivalence structure, whereas rotary encodings substantially restrict the symmetry group. Their analysis connects this reduction to enhanced expressivity and offers a principled explanation for RoPE’s growing use. The positional mechanism therefore affects more than how a model receives information about token order.

The paper also examines linear mode connectivity: how trained solutions relate along straight paths in parameter space. Using an alignment algorithm, the authors empirically show that the existence and variability of this connectivity depend crucially on positional encoding. Together, the results connect an architectural choice to both functional equivalence and the geometry of relationships between Transformer solutions.
icml-2026-functional-equivalence-in-atte.tldr: Positional encodings reshape Transformer symmetries, with RoPE restricting functional equivalences and influencing connectivity between trained solutions.

paragraphs: Estimating how language-model performance scales can require evaluating many checkpoints or drawing many generated samples. Item Response Scaling Laws reduce this burden by separating a model’s latent ability from the characteristics of the questions used to measure it. This lets information be shared across evaluations instead of treating every model-question combination independently.

The framework integrates Item Response Theory with scaling laws, reducing parameter complexity for M models and N questions from a product, O(M × N), to a sum, O(M + N). Its Beta-IRT implementation uses probability-valued responses, including token probabilities and sampled pass rates. These carry more information than recording only a binary success or failure.

The authors validate the approach for both pre-training downstream scaling and test-time scaling. After a one-time calibration using existing responses, they report reliable estimates with just 50 questions per benchmark and comparable or better decision accuracy than traditional approaches. Estimated abilities also support performance forecasting across benchmarks, provided those benchmarks share the same measurement objective. That condition defines the reported scope of cross-benchmark generalization.
icml-2026-item-response-scaling-laws-a-m.tldr: Item Response Scaling Laws separate model ability from question characteristics to estimate scaling efficiently after one-time calibration.

paragraphs: Sparse language models commonly route tokens to selected expert networks, but dynamic hard routing can create hardware inefficiencies and require extra training losses. Large Lookup Layers explore another source of sparsity: embedding tables. Ordinary embeddings efficiently retrieve information by token identity, although that lookup alone does not incorporate context.

L3 extends this idea into decoder layers. Token identity statically selects a set of learned embeddings, and the model combines them in a context-dependent way. This separates which information is retrieved from how it is used in the current sequence. The approach stores information in embeddings to balance memory and computation, supported by an information-theoretic algorithm for allocating embeddings.

The paper also introduces an architecture designed for fast training and CPU-offloaded inference without overhead. Experiments train Transformers with up to 2.6 billion active parameters and report strong improvements over dense models and equally sparse mixtures of experts on language modeling and downstream tasks. These results suggest that static lookup combined with contextual aggregation can provide a competitive route to scaling sparse models.
icml-2026-l-3-large-lookup-layers-c5afa0.tldr: Large Lookup Layers combine static token-based retrieval with contextual embedding aggregation to scale sparse language models efficiently.

paragraphs: Many segmentation systems process an entire image before concentrating on the object of interest. FLIP moves that focus to the input stage. It samples patches at multiple resolutions around a target object, assigning detailed processing to its center while preserving a coarser view of the surrounding scene.

This fovea-inspired design uses patches outside a fixed grid and is designed to handle changes in object scale. The authors evaluate it on five established benchmarks and introduce ObjaScale to test objects spanning an especially wide range of image areas. On that dataset, they report accurate segmentation of very small objects that existing models struggle to handle.

The reported efficiency gains accompany stronger segmentation results. FLIP-Tiny achieves 79.90% mean IoU with 0.51 million parameters, compared with 75.87% for SAM2-L’s 224.45 million parameters. FLIP-Large reaches 83.26% and runs about twice as fast as SAM2-L. The authors also propose object tracking and integration into slot-based scene architectures as promising uses, presenting these as potential extensions of the object-centered design.
icml-2026-looking-locally-object-centric.tldr: FLIP concentrates multiresolution image processing around target objects, achieving strong segmentation accuracy with substantially smaller models.

paragraphs: Quantization compresses a model, but the desired outcome is to preserve its final output distribution. Many methods instead minimize errors in each layer’s immediate activations. This paper argues that such local objectives can be misleading because subsequent layers determine how an intermediate error ultimately affects the prediction.

YAQA, an adaptive rounding algorithm, directly considers error at the network output. The theory first relates rounding convergence time to the structure of Hessian approximations, which describe how the objective curves around parameter settings. It then bounds end-to-end error using the cosine similarity between an approximate Hessian and the true Hessian. This motivates a Kronecker-factored approximation and corresponding near-optimal sketches.

The authors present these as the first end-to-end error bounds for quantization algorithms and establish a provable advantage over GPTQ and LDLQ. Empirically, YAQA reduces error by approximately 30% relative to those methods and even reports lower error than quantization-aware training. The improvements translate into state-of-the-art downstream performance without additional inference overhead, linking the theoretical objective to practical model preservation.
icml-2026-model-preserving-adaptive-roun.tldr: YAQA uses curvature-aware adaptive rounding to control final-output quantization error and improve compressed-model performance without inference overhead.

paragraphs: Link prediction asks which connections should exist in a graph. Strong systems often combine graph neural networks with hand-designed structural signals or large tables of node embeddings. Graph Transformers offer another route, but elaborate structural encodings can add substantial overhead. PENCIL investigates how much a plain Transformer can accomplish with a simpler input design.

The model is an encoder-only Transformer that attends over sampled local subgraphs. This allows attention to extract structural relationships from the sampled neighborhood while retaining standard Transformer hardware efficiency and scalability. The paper’s theoretical and experimental analyses show that PENCIL captures richer structural signals than GNNs and implicitly generalizes a broad class of graph heuristics and subgraph-based expressivity.

Across the reported benchmarks, PENCIL outperforms heuristic-informed GNNs, uses far fewer parameters than alternatives based on node identities, and remains competitive even without node features. The findings suggest that some capabilities associated with elaborate graph-specific engineering can emerge from attention over suitable local inputs. The claim is that simple choices may suffice, rather than that every link-prediction setting benefits equally.
icml-2026-plain-transformers-are-surpris.tldr: PENCIL shows that a plain Transformer attending to sampled local subgraphs can deliver strong, parameter-efficient link prediction.

paragraphs: A poisoned code model can behave normally on ordinary evaluations while generating vulnerable code under particular conditions. Poison-with-Style studies an attack where those conditions are developers’ coding styles. Unlike attacks requiring an adversary to insert a special word into an inference-time prompt, the trigger can already be present in the code a developer naturally supplies.

The proposed attack combines a data-collection method with a two-stage fine-tuning strategy. Its objective is selective behavior: vulnerable completions for prompts containing the trigger style and normal completions for other prompts. The significance is that the triggering signal is embedded in ordinary code presentation, making harmful behavior harder to distinguish through overall code-completion performance alone.

In Python completion experiments, the authors report high success across multiple vulnerabilities and robustness against the evaluated state-of-the-art defenses. One example produces CWE-20 vulnerable code in 95% of triggered cases while reducing HumanEval and MBPP pass@1 by less than 5%. These results demonstrate that strong standard benchmark performance can coexist with style-dependent vulnerabilities in the tested poisoned models.
icml-2026-poison-with-style-a-practical-.tldr: Poison-with-Style uses developers’ coding styles as covert triggers for vulnerable code generation while largely preserving ordinary completion performance.

paragraphs: Recurrent sequence models offer alternatives to the growing compute cost of full attention on long inputs. One way to understand these recurrences is as an online regression process: at each step, the model updates a linear mapping from keys to values. Existing delta-rule updates approximate this process using first-order information while ignoring the curvature of the regression objective.

This paper introduces preconditioning, which adjusts updates to account for that curvature. Starting with online least-squares theory, the authors derive equivalences between linear attention and delta-rule updates in the exactly preconditioned case. They then develop a diagonal approximation that makes the idea practical for DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet, and Kimi Delta Attention.

Efficient chunkwise parallel algorithms accompany the proposed variants, connecting the mathematical formulation to usable sequence computation. Experiments show consistent gains on synthetic recall tasks and language modeling at 340-million- and 1-billion-parameter scales. The results support curvature-aware updates as a way to improve these recurrent models, while distinguishing the exact theoretical equivalence from the diagonal approximation used in practice.
icml-2026-preconditioned-deltanet-curvat.tldr: Preconditioned delta-rule recurrences incorporate regression curvature through efficient diagonal approximations, improving recall and language-modeling results.

paragraphs: Protein language models predict structure and function, but identifying the computations behind those predictions remains difficult. Interpreting each layer independently can reveal features without explaining how information moves through the network. ProtoMech addresses this by learning sparse latent representations jointly across layers using cross-layer transcoders.

The goal is to reconstruct computational circuits rather than produce separate descriptions of individual layers. Applied to ESM2, the framework recovers 82–89% of the original performance on protein-family classification and function-prediction tasks. It also identifies compressed circuits occupying less than 1% of the latent space while retaining up to 79% of model accuracy.

Those circuits correspond to structural and functional motifs associated with binding, signaling, and stability. The authors further use circuit-based steering for protein design, reporting higher fitness than baseline methods in more than 70% of cases. Together, these findings connect interpretability to intervention: the recovered circuits provide a compact account of model behavior and useful directions for influencing generated protein designs in the evaluated setting.
icml-2026-protein-circuit-tracing-via-cr.tldr: ProtoMech traces sparse circuits across protein-model layers and uses them to interpret predictions and steer protein design.

paragraphs: One-bit language models promise lower storage and computation costs, but moving from full-precision weights to binary weights creates a large representational change. This paper argues that the gap makes naive adaptation of an existing model difficult. Training a binary model from scratch avoids that direct transition but incurs substantial training costs and can still suffer accuracy degradation.

The proposed method progressively converts a pretrained model’s weights into binary form. It keeps this transition consistent across both forward computation and backward training updates, making the conversion gradual. Binary-aware initialization and dual-scaling compensation further support the transition, reducing the difficulty of progressive training and improving performance.

Experiments across language models of different sizes report better performance than existing approaches. The stated conclusion is that high-performing one-bit models can be obtained by adapting pretrained models, removing the need for expensive training from scratch in this approach. The contribution therefore concerns the conversion process as much as the compressed representation: it offers a way to retain value from pretraining while making the substantial shift to binary weights.
icml-2026-rethinking-1-bit-optimization-.tldr: A progressive training method converts pretrained language models to one-bit weights and outperforms existing approaches in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Agents that use tools over multiple turns need interactive environments in which to explore and learn. Such environments are scarce, and existing synthesis approaches can struggle to provide sufficient diversity at scale. ScaleEnv addresses this by constructing both interactive environments and verifiable tasks from scratch.

The framework uses procedural testing to establish environment reliability. It expands tool dependency graphs and verifies executable actions to guarantee task completeness and solvability. These mechanisms connect a task’s requirements with the tools and actions available in its environment, making the generated training setting something an agent can actually interact with and solve.

Agents trained through exploration in ScaleEnv show significant improvements on unseen multi-turn tool-use benchmarks, including τ²-Bench and VitaBench. The authors also study how generalization changes as the number of environment domains increases. Their empirical findings identify environmental diversity as an important ingredient for robust learning. The contribution combines environment generation with verification and evidence that broader interactive experience can transfer to unfamiliar tool-use settings.
icml-2026-scaleenv-scaling-environment-s.tldr: ScaleEnv synthesizes verified interactive environments and solvable tasks, improving agents’ generalization to unseen multi-turn tool-use benchmarks.

paragraphs: Full attention becomes expensive as an image’s token count grows, while linear attention can struggle to concentrate on relevant information. This paper studies both within a mathematical framework called generalized attention. Within that framework, the authors prove a dispersion result: as the number of keys tends to infinity, a query’s weights become equal across keys.

SEMA responds by combining token localization with arithmetic averaging. Localization is designed to preserve focus and avoid dispersion, while averaging captures the global aspect of attention in a theoretically consistent way. The architecture draws inspiration from Mamba-style attention and assigns complementary roles to localized processing and global information aggregation.

ImageNet-1k classification experiments support the resulting design as a scalable alternative beyond linear attention. At similar parameter counts, SEMA outperforms recent vision Mamba models as image scales increase. The reported findings connect the theoretical concern about attention losing focus to a practical architectural response, with evidence that combining local concentration and global averaging can improve classification at larger image scales.
icml-2026-sema-a-scalable-and-efficient-.tldr: SEMA combines localized tokens and global averaging to preserve attention focus and improve image classification at increasing scales.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks represent uncertainty over weights, but a standard independent Gaussian posterior requires parameters proportional to the full weight matrix. This paper instead expresses each matrix as a product of two smaller factors. Shared factors introduce structured correlations, and the resulting posterior concentrates on rank-r matrices rather than occupying the full weight space.

The authors motivate this restriction especially when singular values decay quickly, so low-rank structure can capture much of a matrix. Their PAC-Bayes bounds have a complexity term scaling as √(r(m+n)) rather than √(mn). Additional loss bounds separate optimization error from bias caused by restricting rank, and the work extends Gaussian complexity results to Bayesian predictive means.

Experiments across MLPs, LSTMs, and Transformers show competitive predictions with up to 33 times fewer parameters than five-member deep ensembles. The method substantially improves out-of-distribution detection and often improves calibration relative to mean-field and perturbation baselines. Deep ensembles can still perform better on in-distribution likelihood metrics, making the findings a qualified tradeoff between compact uncertainty modeling and different measures of predictive quality.
icml-2026-singular-bayesian-neural-netwo.tldr: Low-rank Bayesian weight posteriors reduce parameter costs while capturing correlations and improving several uncertainty measures in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Policy-guided tree search can tackle difficult deterministic single-agent problems by breaking them into subgoals. Explicitly generating and reasoning over those subgoals, however, can become costly. This paper uses a learned rerooter within the √LTS algorithm to create an implicit decomposition into soft subtasks and direct search effort without reconstructing explicit intermediate goals.

The authors propose three rerooter designs. One uses clustering to capture global structure in the state space. Another uses learned estimates of the remaining cost to reach a goal. A hybrid combines the two sources of information, bringing together the organization of possible states and estimates of progress toward a solution.

Earlier work emphasized formal guarantees for given or handcrafted rerooters; this paper focuses on learning useful designs. Empirically, its methods scale to complex environments where subgoal-based policy tree search fails and achieve state-of-the-art online training efficiency on the tested domains. These results support implicit decomposition as a practical way to allocate search computation while reducing the overhead associated with explicit subgoal management.
icml-2026-structure-induced-information-.tldr: Learned rerooters use state-space structure and cost estimates to guide scalable tree search without explicitly generating subgoals.

paragraphs: A single image-restoration model must handle different forms of damage while preserving both detail and recognizable content. Guidance about degradation alone can be insufficient in heavily damaged regions. Semantic guidance can help reconstruct content, but introducing it into shallow diffusion layers can disrupt spatial structure and produce blur.

TPGDiff assigns three kinds of guidance to complementary roles. Structural priors enter shallow layers to support fine spatial detail, while semantic priors enter deeper layers to guide high-level content. Degradation priors operate throughout the diffusion trajectory, adapting the restoration process across timesteps. This arrangement makes the placement of information within the model part of the restoration strategy.

The structural guidance draws on multiple sources of cues. A distillation-driven extractor supplies robust semantic information even under severe degradation, and a separate degradation extractor provides stage-adaptive control. Experiments on benchmarks with single and multiple degradations report superior performance and generalization across restoration scenarios. The findings support coordinating information about damage, structure, and meaning at the layers and stages where each is intended to help.
icml-2026-tpgdiff-hierarchical-triple-pr.tldr: TPGDiff places structural, semantic, and degradation guidance at complementary layers and timesteps to improve unified image restoration.

paragraphs: Federated fine-tuning must accommodate clients with different computational capacities. Assigning different LoRA ranks helps adapt training, but dense feedforward computation still dominates the cost. This paper explores sparse mixtures of experts as a way to save computation by activating only selected portions of the model.

The authors identify two problems with applying this approach directly: experts receive uneven use, and Top-K routing is non-differentiable. Their convergence analysis links these problems to worse convergence, especially for constrained clients. UB-SMoE introduces Dynamic Modulated Routing to rebalance expert use and Universal Pseudo-Gradient to reconstruct learning signals for experts that were not activated.

The mechanisms are designed to reinforce each other and keep experts viable across heterogeneous clients. Benchmark experiments report up to 45.0% less computation for low-resource clients and an 8.7-fold performance improvement over heterogeneous LoRA-rank methods. The findings indicate that conditional computation needs coordinated routing and learning signals to realize its benefits in federated settings, where participating clients have unequal resources.
icml-2026-ub-smoe-universally-balanced-s.tldr: UB-SMoE balances expert use and restores learning signals to inactive experts, improving federated fine-tuning for resource-constrained clients.

paragraphs: Explaining a time-series classifier can require expensive optimization for every input, and individual explanation methods offer only one attribution perspective. XMA combines several explainers and shifts much of that work into training a separate neural explainer. Once learned, the explainer produces an attribution map through an inference pass.

For each training instance, the framework selects the expert map with the best combined faithfulness and robustness score. The student learns from this instance-specific choice while also directly optimizing differentiable versions of those objectives, allowing refinement beyond an individual teacher. A segmentation procedure then converts pointwise attributions into contiguous time segments without changing their faithfulness score.

Across three classifier architectures, XMA achieves the best AUPRC among compared methods on four synthetic datasets and MIT-ECG with cardiologist-verified ground truth. On eleven multivariate UEA datasets, it leads in faithfulness on seven and robustness on eight. These results support learning from complementary explainers while preserving a lightweight inference path, with the strongest explanation method allowed to vary by input.
icml-2026-unified-time-series-explanatio.tldr: XMA learns a fast time-series explainer from instance-specific expert choices and directly optimizes explanation faithfulness and robustness.

paragraphs: Different image degradations can demand conflicting restoration behavior, making a single unified model difficult to optimize. UDBM treats restoration as stochastic transport guided by uncertainty at individual pixels. This gives the model a finer basis for adapting its restoration process than coarse control mechanisms or fixed mapping schedules.

The method relaxes the terminal constraint in a diffusion bridge, replacing a strict endpoint requirement with a relaxed one. This formulation models uncertainty in the degradations and theoretically resolves the drift singularity present in standard diffusion bridges. The paper then introduces two complementary controls: a noise schedule that brings different degradations into a shared high-entropy latent space, and a path schedule that adaptively controls the transport trajectory.

The path design is motivated by the viscous dynamics of entropy regularization. Together, these components modify both the geometry of the transformation and how it proceeds. The authors report state-of-the-art results across diverse restoration tasks using a single inference step, connecting uncertainty-aware transport modeling with an efficient unified restoration procedure.
icml-2026-unifying-heterogeneous-degrada.tldr: UDBM uses pixelwise uncertainty and a relaxed diffusion bridge to unify diverse image-restoration tasks in one inference step.
